r: In the 2022 UK pilot, 61 companies and about 2,900 employees tried a shorter schedule for six months. Afterward, 56 firms kept it, and revenue barely changed. These numbers make the idea look better than it may be, because the firms volunteered. Volunteers tend to be knowledge-work companies, and their calendars are full of meetings that are easy to cut. Iceland's public-sector trials, which ran from 2015 to 2019 and covered about 2,500 workers, suggest a different source of the gain. The benefit seems to come less from fewer hours than from a forced review of the calendar, which ends the "Friday tax" that leaders have never been willing to stop paying. Teams should pilot the shorter week where output, not presence, defines value. Customer support rotations and on-call incident response plans rarely survive compression without extra staff. Here is the test: if a team cannot cut meetings enough to reach 32 hours within one quarter, the four-day week becomes a pay cut disguised as a perk.
